metadata.title: Predicting-Academic-Performance-of-Immigrant-Stude
metadata.venue: International Journal of Information Technology and Web Engineering

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses OECD PISA microdata for 15-year-old students, focusing on immigrant students in five economies (UAE, Qatar, Canada, Spain, Australia) and using questionnaire-derived derived variables plus cognitive outcomes. The manuscript states that “each student is allocated specific weight for syncing the sample with the true population,” but it does not report the exact PISA weight variable name or whether the authors applied it in the ML training/evaluation pipeline. Because the models are standard regression ML methods (XGBoost regressor and other regressors) implemented in Python with scaling and GridSearchCV, the paper does not document any complex survey design handling (stratification/clustering/replicate weights) during model fitting. Analysts should, for replication, apply the appropriate PISA student sampling weight (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) and ensure that any preprocessing (e.g., scaling) is performed within cross-validation folds to avoid leakage.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are PISA plausible values (PV1MATH, PV1READ, PV1SCIE) for cognitive domains, but the paper does not describe how missing questionnaire/test-derived variables were handled before model training. This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically contain missingness in background variables and ML pipelines are sensitive to whether missing cases are removed or imputed. Without the missing-data strategy, it is unclear whether performance differences reflect model quality or differences in the analytic sample composition.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study performs secondary analysis using OECD PISA 2018 administration data (the manuscript also references “PISA 2015 dataset” in the EDM description, but the explicit data section states 2018 administration). It constructs a cleaned dataset with immigrant students restricted to five economies: UAE, Qatar, Canada, Spain, and Australia. The target is set separately for each cognitive domain by using PV1MATH, PV1SCIE, or PV1READ as the regression outcome and dropping the other two PVs when training each target-specific model. The paper also applies preprocessing including standard scaling and uses GridSearchCV with k-fold cross-validation; however, it does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion rules (e.g., minimum item response, missingness thresholds, or whether only complete cases were retained).

main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost regressor after hyperparameter tuning: RMSE=75.7679, RSE=0.4201, MAPE=12.8402. Best comparison: Random Forest RMSE=79.9549, RSE=0.3543, MAPE=14.7879; XGBoost before tuning RMSE=79.2638, RSE=0.3654, MAPE=14.6033. Linear Regression RMSE=83.9068; SVM RMSE=84.3194; Extra Trees RMSE=81.3275.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (immigrant students) the study leveraged immigration status, books at home, computer access for school work, math learning time, and grade repetition to predict mathematics achievement (PV1MATH), finding that XGBoost regressor with hyperparameter tuning achieved the lowest error (RMSE=75.7679; MAPE=12.8402) compared with linear regression, SVM, random forest, and extra trees. This indicates that gradient-boosted tree models with tuned hyperparameters may improve predictive accuracy for immigrant students’ mathematics performance, supporting targeted data-driven interventions, though the paper does not document survey-weight use or missing-data handling.

main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost regressor after hyperparameter tuning: RMSE=74.2779, RSE=0.4341, MAPE=12.5953. Best comparison: Random Forest RMSE=79.2575, RSE=0.3727, MAPE=14.4692; XGBoost before tuning RMSE=78.9523, RSE=0.3776, MAPE=14.4024. Linear Regression RMSE=83.7414; SVM RMSE=83.9915; Extra Trees RMSE=81.1393.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (immigrant students) the study leveraged immigration status, books at home, digital device access for science, science learning time, and physical infrastructure constraints to predict science achievement (PV1SCIE), finding that XGBoost regressor with hyperparameter tuning produced the lowest prediction errors (RMSE=74.2779; MAPE=12.5953) relative to the other tested regressors. This indicates that tuned XGBoost models can provide more accurate forecasts of immigrant students’ science performance, which may help schools prioritize instructional and resource supports, while causality cannot be inferred from predictive error reductions and the paper does not report missing-data or weighting procedures.

main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost regressor after hyperparameter tuning: RMSE=77.3599, RSE=0.4626, MAPE=13.5346. Best comparison: Random Forest RMSE=84.1115, RSE=0.3963, MAPE=15.5758; XGBoost before tuning RMSE=82.7236, RSE=0.4161, MAPE=15.3459. Linear Regression RMSE=88.8190; SVM RMSE=89.2674; Extra Trees RMSE=86.2125.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 (immigrant students) the study leveraged immigration status, study environment (quiet place to study), reading-related behaviors (fluent reading and re-reading before understanding), and school language support (additional language lessons) to predict reading achievement (PV1READ), finding that XGBoost regressor with hyperparameter tuning achieved the lowest error (RMSE=77.3599; MAPE=13.5346) among the evaluated models. This indicates that machine-learning-based prediction of reading performance for immigrant students may enable earlier identification of students at risk and more timely instructional support, though the study’s transparency on survey weights and missing-data handling is limited.

data.outcome_summary: The study conducts educational data mining on OECD PISA 2018 microdata for immigrant students in five economies (UAE, Qatar, Canada, Spain, Australia), predicting cognitive outcomes using PISA plausible values (PV1MATH, PV1SCIE, PV1READ). For each domain, the authors train regression models and compare Linear Regression, SVM, Ridge, Random Forest, Extra Trees, and XGBoost, then fine-tune XGBoost using GridSearchCV with k-fold cross-validation. Across Mathematics, Science, and Reading, XGBoost after hyperparameter tuning yields the lowest errors, with RMSE improving from about 79→75.77 (Math), 78.95→74.28 (Science), and 82.72→77.36 (Reading), and MAPE dropping to 12.84, 12.60, and 13.53 respectively. The paper does not report the exact survey weight variable used in ML training, nor does it document missing-data handling, which limits interpretability and generalizability. Additionally, the results are predictive performance metrics rather than causal effects.
